vignette:
He remembers the day clearly, though he wishes he didn’t. It was a Tuesday, five years ago now, and the sky had been a dirty gray over the Gulf of Thailand. He and his youngest son, Chai, had been out on their boat since before dawn, hauling nets heavy with mackerel. The wind picked up fast, turning the sea from flat glass to rolling hills of dark water. Chai was twenty-one then, strong and sure-footed, but when the wave hit—a rogue wall that came without warning—he lost his footing on the wet deck and went over the side. The boat pitched, the engine sputtered, and by the time his father cut the throttle and dove in, the water was already closing over Chai’s head. He swam until his arms burned, but the current was too strong, the visibility too poor. He never found him. The Coast Guard recovered the body two days later.

Mr. Nguyen still goes out on the water. He has to—fishing is all he knows, and there is no pension, no other work. But he no longer takes the same route. He avoids the stretch of coast where Chai went under, even if it means longer hours and smaller catches. His wife, Somsak, has started packing his lunch the night before, but he often forgets to eat. He sits in the stern, staring at the horizon, his hands gripping the wheel so hard that his knuckles blanch. The sound of a sudden splash—a dolphin, a piece of debris—sends his heart slamming against his ribs. He will scan the water for minutes afterward, his mouth dry, his breath shallow, until he convinces himself there is nothing there.

At night, he dreams. The dreams are not always the same, but they always feature Chai. In one, he sees his son standing on the dock, waving, but when Mr. Nguyen reaches him, Chai’s face dissolves into seawater. In another, he is drowning himself, unable to scream, and the weight of the ocean presses down until he wakes gasping, tangled in sweat-soaked sheets. Somsak reaches for him sometimes, but he cannot bear to be touched. He lies rigid, staring at the ceiling, watching the fan blades trace their endless circles.

His memory has become unreliable. He will forget where he left his gear, or why he walked into the kitchen. But the details of that day are etched in perfect clarity: the color of Chai’s shirt (a faded blue), the sound of his last shout, the salt on Mr. Nguyen’s lips as he gulped air between dives. He replays it like a film he cannot stop, and each time he asks himself the same useless question: *Why didn’t I tie him to a line? Why didn’t we stay in port?* He knows the answer—the storm came too fast, Chai was an experienced fisherman—but the guilt sits in his chest like a stone, heavy and permanent.

His temper has shortened. Last month, a deckhand accidentally dropped a crate of squid on the deck, and Mr. Nguyen screamed at him for ten minutes—loud, raw, the kind of shouting he used to associate with other men, not himself. Later, he apologized, but the shame lingered. He does not laugh as much as he used to. He does not tell stories at the dock. He keeps to himself, even when other fishermen call out greetings. The sea, which once felt like a partner, now feels like an enemy he must endure.

Somsak has noticed. She tells him gently that he is not the same man she married. He knows she is right, but he does not know how to become that man again. He comes to therapy reluctantly, because she insisted, because he cannot keep living this way: half-present, half-drowning on dry land. He sits in the chair across from me, his hands folded, his eyes fixed on a spot just past my shoulder. He speaks in a voice that is soft and careful, as if the words themselves might break something inside him. And when he finishes telling me about that Tuesday, he falls silent, and the room fills with the sound of a man breathing around a grief that will not let go.
